title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
body:
An **eigenvector** of a square [[Matrix]] $A$ is a non-zero vector whose direction $A$ does not
change. Applying $A$ only stretches or shrinks it:

$$
A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}
$$

The scalar $\lambda$ is the **eigenvalue**: the factor by which that direction gets scaled.
"Eigen" is German for "own", so these are the matrix's own directions.

**Why anyone cares:** a [[Linear Transformation]] in general moves every vector somewhere
unrelated, and reasoning about it means tracking all of that at once. The eigenvectors are the
handful of directions where it does something trivial. Find them and you have found the axes the
transformation is *really* built around, in which it is nothing but a set of independent
stretches. Everything from [[Diagonalization]] to PCA to solving systems of ODEs is that one
observation, cashed in.

Note $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$ is required, or the equation would be satisfied trivially by
every $\lambda$. **$\lambda = 0$ is allowed**, and it means something specific: $A\mathbf{v} =
\mathbf{0}$ for a non-zero $\mathbf{v}$, so $A$ is singular and has a non-trivial
[[Kernel and Range|kernel]].

## Finding them

Rearrange, using $I$ so the shapes work:

$$
A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}
\;\iff\;
A\mathbf{v} - \lambda I\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\;\iff\;
(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
$$

This is a homogeneous [[System of Linear Equations]], and we need a **non-zero** solution. From
the equivalence table in [[Matrix Inverse]], that happens exactly when $A - \lambda I$ is
singular, which happens exactly when its [[Determinant]] vanishes:

$$
\det(A - \lambda I) = 0
$$

That is the **characteristic equation**. Expanding the determinant gives the **characteristic
polynomial**, of degree $n$ in $\lambda$, and its roots are the eigenvalues. **This is the
determinant's most important job in the course.**

Then for each eigenvalue, plug it back in and solve $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ by
[[Gaussian Elimination]]. The solution set is the **eigenspace** for $\lambda$: a subspace, not
a single vector, since any scalar multiple of an eigenvector is another eigenvector. What you
report is a [[Basis]] for it.

## Worked example

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\det(A - \lambda I) = \det\begin{bmatrix} 4-\lambda & 1 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
= (4-\lambda)(3-\lambda) - 2 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda-5)(\lambda-2)
$$

so $\lambda = 5$ and $\lambda = 2$.

For $\lambda = 5$: $(A - 5I) = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, giving $-v_1 +
v_2 = 0$, so $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ (up to scale).

For $\lambda = 2$: $(A - 2I) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, giving $2v_1 + v_2
= 0$, so $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$.

**Sanity checks that catch most arithmetic slips**: the eigenvalues sum to the trace (the
diagonal sum, $4 + 3 = 7 = 5 + 2$) and multiply to the determinant ($12 - 2 = 10 = 5 \times 2$).
Both are free and both are worth doing every time.

## Facts

- **Only square matrices have eigenvalues.** A non-square matrix maps between different spaces,
  so "same direction out as in" is not a question you can ask. (The generalisation that handles
  rectangular matrices is the [[Singular Value Decomposition]], which asks for an input direction
  and an output direction instead of one.)
- An $n \times n$ matrix has **$n$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity**, by the fundamental
  theorem of algebra, but some may be repeated and some may be complex.
- **Complex eigenvalues mean rotation.** A rotation matrix leaves no real direction fixed, and
  its characteristic polynomial has no real roots. This is where [[Complex Numbers]] stop being
  a strange appendix to the course and start being necessary, and it is why they are on this
  syllabus at all.
- **Symmetric matrices ($A^T = A$) always have real eigenvalues** and eigenvectors that are
  mutually orthogonal. That is the [[Spectral Theorem]], and it is what makes
  [[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]] work, since a covariance matrix is symmetric.
- Triangular matrices hand you the eigenvalues for free: they are the diagonal entries.
- Eigenvectors for **distinct** eigenvalues are always
  [[Linear Dependence|linearly independent]], which is the key input to [[Diagonalization]].
- $A^k$ has eigenvalues $\lambda^k$ with the same eigenvectors. Repeated application just
  repeats the stretch, which is the whole trick behind fast matrix powers.

## Applications

- **[[Diagonalization]]**, the immediate one: use the eigenvectors as a [[Basis]] and $A$ becomes
  diagonal.
- **Systems of differential equations.** $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ has solutions
  $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$ for each eigenpair, so eigenvalues decide whether the system decays,
  grows, or oscillates: negative real parts decay, positive grow, imaginary parts oscillate.
  This is the "basic science application" on the syllabus and it is where
  [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] picks the material up. See [[Systems of Differential Equations]], which
  is that course's version of this bullet, and [[Phase Portrait]] for reading stability off the
  eigenvalues without solving anything.
- **Population and Markov models.** Repeated application of a transition matrix converges to the
  eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, the steady state. PageRank is this, on the web's link
  [[Graph]].
- **[[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]] and dimensionality reduction.** The eigenvectors of a
  covariance matrix are the directions of greatest variance, ordered by eigenvalue. Keep the top
  few and you have compressed the data with the least possible loss, which
  [[Low-Rank Approximation|Eckart-Young-Mirsky]] makes precise. **Nothing else in the vault
  reaches [[MACHINE LEARNING]] as directly as this**, and it runs through
  [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303).
